If you follow a team outside Los Angeles, this is the part of the schedule worth checking.Read More →Posted September 26, 2026The Different Leagues of College FootballCollege football feels different depending on the conference, the school, and the traditions. You can plan a special dinner with a view, sit down for a tasting menu, grab a relaxed neighborhood meal, or meet friends somewhere lively without making the night about a long drive across Los Angeles. The Valley is spread out, so the easiest way to explore it is to think about the kind of experience you want first, then choose the neighborhood.Read More →Posted September 24, 2026Halloween Activities in and Around the San Fernando ValleyHalloween outings around the Valley range from glowing pumpkin displays to outdoor movies and community celebrations. before.text: Moving TimelineChoosing a Home Purchase Timeline Around MarriageThere's no universal right answer to this, since it depends on where a couple is in their relationship, their finances, and how much legal complexity they're comfortable navigating before a wedding takes place.Read MoreHome TitleChoosing Home Title for Unmarried BuyersUnmarried buyers can choose a title arrangement that reflects their intended ownership, contributions, and inheritance wishes. The title choice is separate from the mortgage application and should be reviewed with an attorney before the deed is recorded.Read MoreBuying DecisionManaging Shared Finances Before Buying a Home TogetherYou do not need to merge every account before buying a home together. You do need a clear understanding of purchase contributions, ongoing payments, savings, and the lender’s documentation requirements.Read MoreDivorce PlanningUnderstanding a Shared Home if the Marriage Later EndsIf you divorce later, the house may be kept by one person, sold, or handled another way under the divorce agreement and applicable property law. Buying a home together before or during marriage means thinking ahead to a scenario neither partner wants to imagine, what happens to the house if the marriage ends.Read MoreCredit PlanningJoint Home Buying When Only One Partner Has Strong CreditTwo people may be able to buy together with different credit profiles, but the financing options depend on how the lender evaluates each borrower. A joint application and an application by one borrower can produce different results and different ownership considerations.Read MoreBuying DecisionComparing Buying and Renting While Settling Into Married LifeBuying together may suit a couple with a lasting location plan, suitable financing, and a clear agreement about the home’s responsibilities. Continuing to rent can provide flexibility while work, finances, or shared priorities are still changing.Read MoreAffordabilityHome Buying for Newlyweds With Student Loan DebtNewlyweds can still buy a home with student loan debt by choosing a payment and price range that work after the lender counts the required debt payments. Combining two incomes as a newly married couple can help offset the impact of student loan debt on affordability, but it requires understanding exactly how that debt factors into mortgage qualification.Read MorePrenuptial PlanningPrenuptial Agreements and Buying a Home TogetherA prenuptial agreement can help clarify property and financial expectations before marriage, including a planned home purchase. Whether it is appropriate and enforceable requires advice from qualified attorneys rather than a real estate recommendation.Read MoreBuying TogetherChoosing a Starter Home as a Newly Married CoupleA good starter home is one you can comfortably afford now and live in long enough to make the purchase worthwhile, without needing it to be your forever home. A starter home doesn't need to be a couple's forever home, but choosing well still requires thinking beyond just the immediate present.Read MoreMortgage PlanningJoint Mortgage Qualification for Unmarried BuyersYou do not have to be married to apply for a joint mortgage. Each applicant still needs to meet the lender’s requirements, and a separate ownership agreement can clarify contributions and responsibilities between unmarried buyers.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing a Home Purchase Before and After the WeddingPut both goals on one cash flow plan. Compare the wedding budget, cash needed to buy, emergency savings, and the monthly payment you can handle after the wedding so one goal does not weaken the other.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together When One Spouse Already Has a MortgageA prior mortgage can affect the debt used for qualification and the cash available for the next purchase. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together With Different Credit Scores or DebtsYou may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home PurchaseMarried couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The lender also reviews debts, credit, assets, and the property, so two incomes do not automatically mean approval.Read MoreLife ChangesChoosing a Home When Combining HouseholdsStart with the people who will live there and the routines the home must support: bedrooms, privacy, work or school needs, storage, transportation, outdoor space, and the monthly cost. A larger home is useful only if it solves the household’s real day to day needs.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing a Starter Home With a Home for a Growing FamilyCompare the cost of moving twice with the cost of buying for the next stage now. The best choice depends on how certain your timing, location, budget, and space needs are, not only on the number of bedrooms.Read MoreLife ChangesUnderstanding Home Title Without Being on the MortgageBeing named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Not being named on the mortgage loan generally means you are not one of the borrowers personally responsible for making the loan payments, although the lender’s lien can still affect the property.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering Adding a Spouse to Your Home’s TitleTitle and the mortgage do different things: title reflects ownership, while the mortgage identifies who owes the lender. Do not treat adding a spouse to title as a routine form; understand the ownership, lending, and tax consequences first.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing Renting and Buying as NewlywedsBuying tends to make more sense when your income, location, savings, and expected time in the area are stable enough to justify the upfront and ongoing costs. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying a Home Together Before MarriageGetting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Buying afterward can make sense when your shared budget, savings, location, and expected time in the home support the purchase. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.Read MoreLife ChangesCombining Households When Both Partners Own HomesYou do not automatically have to sell both homes. Compare each property's equity, mortgage, rental potential, tax consequences and how much cash you need for the next purchase before deciding what to keep or sell.Read MoreLife ChangesPlanning a Home Purchase for a Growing FamilyThink beyond one extra bedroom. Prioritize the space, storage, commute, childcare routine, outdoor needs, and monthly payment that will support your family for the years you expect to stay.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Equity From a Home Owned Before MarriageIn California, a home owned before marriage generally begins as separate property. That starting point does not settle every later question: changes to title, agreements, and the use of marital funds can affect the analysis. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint PurchaseOption 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.Read MoreLife ChangesFinding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a CoupleStart with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. That gives you a usable price range instead of confusing a lender’s maximum approval with a comfortable budget.Read More

before.text: Moving TimelineChoosing a Home Purchase Timeline Around MarriageThere's no universal right answer to this, since it depends on where a couple is in their relationship, their finances, and how much legal complexity they're comfortable navigating before a wedding takes place.Read MoreHome TitleChoosing Home Title for Unmarried BuyersUnmarried buyers can choose a title arrangement that reflects their intended ownership, contributions, and inheritance wishes. The title choice is separate from the mortgage application and should be reviewed with an attorney before the deed is recorded.Read MoreBuying DecisionManaging Shared Finances Before Buying a Home TogetherYou do not need to merge every account before buying a home together. You do need a clear understanding of purchase contributions, ongoing payments, savings, and the lender’s documentation requirements.Read MoreDivorce PlanningUnderstanding a Shared Home if the Marriage Later EndsIf you divorce later, the house may be kept by one person, sold, or handled another way under the divorce agreement and applicable property law. Buying a home together before or during marriage means thinking ahead to a scenario neither partner wants to imagine, what happens to the house if the marriage ends.Read MoreCredit PlanningJoint Home Buying When Only One Partner Has Strong CreditTwo people may be able to buy together with different credit profiles, but the financing options depend on how the lender evaluates each borrower. A joint application and an application by one borrower can produce different results and different ownership considerations.Read MoreBuying DecisionComparing Buying and Renting While Settling Into Married LifeBuying together may suit a couple with a lasting location plan, suitable financing, and a clear agreement about the home’s responsibilities. Continuing to rent can provide flexibility while work, finances, or shared priorities are still changing.Read MoreAffordabilityHome Buying for Newlyweds With Student Loan DebtNewlyweds can still buy a home with student loan debt by choosing a payment and price range that work after the lender counts the required debt payments. Combining two incomes as a newly married couple can help offset the impact of student loan debt on affordability, but it requires understanding exactly how that debt factors into mortgage qualification.Read MorePrenuptial PlanningPrenuptial Agreements and Buying a Home TogetherA prenuptial agreement can help clarify property and financial expectations before marriage, including a planned home purchase. Whether it is appropriate and enforceable requires advice from qualified attorneys rather than a real estate recommendation.Read MoreBuying TogetherChoosing a Starter Home as a Newly Married CoupleA good starter home is one you can comfortably afford now and live in long enough to make the purchase worthwhile, without needing it to be your forever home. A starter home doesn't need to be a couple's forever home, but choosing well still requires thinking beyond just the immediate present.Read MoreMortgage PlanningJoint Mortgage Qualification for Unmarried BuyersYou do not have to be married to apply for a joint mortgage. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together With Different Credit Scores or DebtsYou may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home PurchaseMarried couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The best choice depends on how certain your timing, location, budget, and space needs are, not only on the number of bedrooms.Read MoreLife ChangesUnderstanding Home Title Without Being on the MortgageBeing named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying a Home Together Before MarriageGetting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.Read MoreLife ChangesCombining Households When Both Partners Own HomesYou do not automatically have to sell both homes. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint PurchaseOption 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.Read MoreLife ChangesFinding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a CoupleStart with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. Combining two incomes as a newly married couple can help offset the impact of student loan debt on affordability, but it requires understanding exactly how that debt factors into mortgage qualification.Read MorePrenuptial PlanningPrenuptial Agreements and Buying a Home TogetherA prenuptial agreement can help clarify property and financial expectations before marriage, including a planned home purchase. Whether it is appropriate and enforceable requires advice from qualified attorneys rather than a real estate recommendation.Read MoreBuying TogetherChoosing a Starter Home as a Newly Married CoupleA good starter home is one you can comfortably afford now and live in long enough to make the purchase worthwhile, without needing it to be your forever home. A starter home doesn't need to be a couple's forever home, but choosing well still requires thinking beyond just the immediate present.Read MoreMortgage PlanningJoint Mortgage Qualification for Unmarried BuyersYou do not have to be married to apply for a joint mortgage. Each applicant still needs to meet the lender’s requirements, and a separate ownership agreement can clarify contributions and responsibilities between unmarried buyers.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing a Home Purchase Before and After the WeddingPut both goals on one cash flow plan. Compare the wedding budget, cash needed to buy, emergency savings, and the monthly payment you can handle after the wedding so one goal does not weaken the other.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together When One Spouse Already Has a MortgageA prior mortgage can affect the debt used for qualification and the cash available for the next purchase. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together With Different Credit Scores or DebtsYou may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home PurchaseMarried couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The lender also reviews debts, credit, assets, and the property, so two incomes do not automatically mean approval.Read MoreLife ChangesChoosing a Home When Combining HouseholdsStart with the people who will live there and the routines the home must support: bedrooms, privacy, work or school needs, storage, transportation, outdoor space, and the monthly cost. A larger home is useful only if it solves the household’s real day to day needs.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing a Starter Home With a Home for a Growing FamilyCompare the cost of moving twice with the cost of buying for the next stage now. The best choice depends on how certain your timing, location, budget, and space needs are, not only on the number of bedrooms.Read MoreLife ChangesUnderstanding Home Title Without Being on the MortgageBeing named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Not being named on the mortgage loan generally means you are not one of the borrowers personally responsible for making the loan payments, although the lender’s lien can still affect the property.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering Adding a Spouse to Your Home’s TitleTitle and the mortgage do different things: title reflects ownership, while the mortgage identifies who owes the lender. Do not treat adding a spouse to title as a routine form; understand the ownership, lending, and tax consequences first.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing Renting and Buying as NewlywedsBuying tends to make more sense when your income, location, savings, and expected time in the area are stable enough to justify the upfront and ongoing costs. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying a Home Together Before MarriageGetting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Buying afterward can make sense when your shared budget, savings, location, and expected time in the home support the purchase. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.Read MoreLife ChangesCombining Households When Both Partners Own HomesYou do not automatically have to sell both homes. Compare each property's equity, mortgage, rental potential, tax consequences and how much cash you need for the next purchase before deciding what to keep or sell.Read MoreLife ChangesPlanning a Home Purchase for a Growing FamilyThink beyond one extra bedroom. Prioritize the space, storage, commute, childcare routine, outdoor needs, and monthly payment that will support your family for the years you expect to stay.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Equity From a Home Owned Before MarriageIn California, a home owned before marriage generally begins as separate property. That starting point does not settle every later question: changes to title, agreements, and the use of marital funds can affect the analysis. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint PurchaseOption 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.Read MoreLife ChangesFinding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a CoupleStart with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. That gives you a usable price range instead of confusing a lender’s maximum approval with a comfortable budget.Read More
